# Prompt 16: Critical technical review of the draft (`paper/main.pdf`, 11 pages)

**Provenance:** This review was generated by the AI assistant (Claude Code), acting as a critical reviewer of its own draft, as Prompt 16 instructs. It is **not** a review by a human peer. It is not presented as one, and it should not be cited as external review.

## Summary judgement

This is a carefully validated, honestly reported course-level study. Its central claim, that conclusions flip across equivalent prompts for most abstracts, is well supported *for the two models tested*. The main threats are external validity (two very weak models) and a scoring protocol that forces a label when the model would not naturally give one.

| M1 | §3.2, §4.1, §6 | Both models are close to the majority class (B1 ≈ MAJ for Llama, p = 0.45). Instability in near-chance models may simply reflect the absence of an evidence-driven signal. | The headline claim could be read as being about LLMs in general | Done: §4.1 and §6 state this explicitly. **Still open:** run Qwen2.5-1.5B or a ≥ 7B model with the frozen protocol |
| M2 | §3.4, §4.3 | Restricted scoring forces a yes/no/maybe choice even when label mass is low (0.00–0.38 for the underspecified prompts). The underspecified-family results, and H2, rest on forced choices. | H2's "contradicted" verdict may be an artifact of the protocol | Done: caveat added in §4.3 and §6. **Open:** report family results restricted to items with label mass > 0.5, or use generation with a parser |
| M3 | §4.4 | The calibration mechanism ("the empty input has a correct answer") is an inference. No experiment isolates it. | The paper's most novel interpretive claim is untested | Done: framed as an inference, as a boundary condition. **Open:** calibrate over {yes, no} only, or use content-free inputs paired with an unanswerable question |
| M4 | §3.6 | The sampling-variance comparison samples from the restricted 3-way distribution, not from real decoding. | "Prompt variance ≈ sampling variance" might not hold under free-text sampling | Done: stated in Limitations |
| M5 | §3.7, D9 | The decision thresholds were written after dev accuracies for one model had been seen. | Mild risk to the "pre-specified" claim | Done: disclosed in the paper and in `research_decisions.md`. ## MINOR concerns

| # | Location | Concern | Remedy |
|---|---|---|---|
| m1 | Table 2 | McNemar tests are run for 7 comparisons per model without multiplicity correction | ENS-para for Llama (p = 0.027) would not survive Bonferroni (α = 0.007). Fixed in §4.4 |
| m2 | §4.2 | "Agreement at chance level (κ = 0.11, −0.10)": κ near 0 means *no agreement beyond chance*. The wording is fine, but κ is depressed when one label dominates (the kappa paradox) | Optional: add a footnote |
| m3 | Figure 4 | The "all 14" bars are near 100% by construction (more prompts means more chances to flip) | The caption could note that flip rate increases with K. Families with equal K remain comparable |
| m4 | §2 | The comparison with Hariprasad 2026 and Sadanandan 2026 relies on their abstracts only (OpenAlex) | **Action for the author:** read both papers in full before submission |
| m5 | Table 2 | Bootstrap CIs and McNemar tests use the same 500 items; CIs for derived methods are not adjusted for selection on dev | Acceptable; B2 is the only selected method, and it was selected on dev |
| m6 | §3.2 | Model licences are given only in the repository README | Optional: add them to the paper |

## Unsupported claims check

- **Novelty:** the paper explicitly does not claim to be the first. ✔
- **Generalisation:** the Discussion and Conclusion restrict claims to small models. ✔
- **Performance:** ensemble gains are reported with tests and CIs. ✔ (see m1)
- **Every number in the text** was checked against `results/tables/*.csv` by the AI after writing. Three phrasing errors were found and fixed before compilation:
  - the calibration "×20 / ×300 boost" wording became "weights 1/p̂_cf ≈ 20 / ≈ 330"
  - "pre-registered" became "pre-specified"
  - the prompt count went from 13 to 14
